title: Zephaniah 1:1–13
context: Zephaniah 1:1–13 opens with the LORD’s word to Zephaniah, whose family line is traced back four generations to a Hezekiah, possibly the king, in the days of King Josiah of Judah (roughly the later seventh century BC, with exact dates uncertain). The LORD announces that he will sweep away everything from the face of the earth, then narrows the focus to Judah and Jerusalem: worshipers of Baal, of the army of the sky, and of Malcam alongside the LORD, and those who have turned away or never sought him. The prophet calls for silence before the Lord GOD because the day of the LORD is near and the LORD has prepared a sacrifice. The LORD will punish princes, the king’s sons, the violent and deceitful, the merchants of the city, and the complacent who say the LORD will do neither good nor evil. He will search Jerusalem with lamps, and their houses and vineyards will be lost. Josiah’s reforms (2 Kings 22–23) form the likely background, though how the prophecy relates to them in time is uncertain. Shared ground: both traditions read the unit as a sober warning against mixed worship and practical unbelief, spoken to God’s own people.

verses.text: The LORD’s word which came to Zephaniah, the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah, the son of Amon, king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The book opens with the LORD’s word to Zephaniah in the days of Josiah, tracing his ancestry back to Hezekiah. Arminian readers see God speaking through a named prophet at a specific moment in Judah’s history, calling his people to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s word coming at his appointed time. Both traditions note that the Hezekiah named here may be the king, though this is not certain, and that Josiah’s reforms (2 Kings 22–23) are the likely backdrop.

verses.text: I will utterly sweep away everything from the surface of the earth, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will utterly sweep away everything from the face of the earth. Arminian readers see a sweeping announcement of judgment that shows the seriousness of sin and God’s authority over all creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign right to judge the whole earth. Both traditions note that the language echoes the flood (Genesis 6:7), and they read the universal scope as setting the stage for the focus on Judah.

verses.text: I will sweep away man and animal. I will sweep away the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. I will cut off man from the surface of the earth, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will sweep away people, animals, birds, and fish, and cut off humanity from the earth. Arminians see creation itself affected by human sin, reversing the order of Genesis 1 in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal of creation as a sign of judgment’s seriousness. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note that the heaps of rubble with the wicked are read in different ways.

verses.text: I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. I will cut off the remnant of Baal from this place—the name of the idolatrous and pagan priests,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will stretch out his hand against Judah and Jerusalem and cut off the remnant of Baal and the idolatrous priests. Arminian readers see God turning judgment toward his own people, who were mixing the worship of Baal with his worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God purifying his people from idolatry. Both traditions note that the remnant of Baal may suggest that Josiah’s reforms had begun but not finished, and they hold the timing loosely.

verses.text: those who worship the army of the sky on the housetops, those who worship and swear by the LORD and also swear by Malcam,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD names those who worship the army of the sky on rooftops and swear by the LORD and also by Malcam. Arminians see divided worship as a betrayal of the LORD, who alone deserves loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see mixed worship as unfaithfulness. Both traditions note that Malcam is likely Milcom or Molech, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5), and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: those who have turned back from following the LORD, and those who haven’t sought the LORD nor inquired after him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD names those who turned back from following him and those who never sought or inquired of him. Arminian readers see both falling away and indifference as serious failures in a people called to seek God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing both apostasy and spiritual neglect. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: not seeking the LORD is itself a form of turning from him.

verses.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord GOD, for the day of the LORD is at hand. For the LORD has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
verses.arminianNotes: Zephaniah calls for silence before the Lord GOD, for the day of the LORD is near, and the LORD has prepared a sacrifice and consecrated his guests. Arminians see a solemn call to reverence before God’s coming judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony that Judah, expecting to be a guest, becomes the sacrifice. Both traditions note that the consecrated guests may be the invading nations called to carry out judgment, and they hold the image soberly.

verses.text: It will happen in the day of the LORD’s sacrifice that I will punish the princes, the king’s sons, and all those who are clothed with foreign clothing.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that on the day of his sacrifice he will punish the princes, the king’s sons, and those in foreign clothing. Arminian readers see the leaders held responsible for leading the nation away from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see judgment beginning with those in authority. Both traditions note that foreign clothing likely signals adopting pagan customs, and they read the verse as a warning against conformity to idolatry.

verses.text: In that day, I will punish all those who leap over the threshold, who fill their master’s house with violence and deceit.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will punish those who leap over the threshold and fill their master’s house with violence and deceit. Arminians see superstition and injustice joined together, as the people followed pagan customs and oppressed others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see violence and deceit as signs of a corrupt society. Both traditions note that leaping over the threshold may refer to a pagan custom (compare 1 Samuel 5:5), though its meaning is uncertain.

verses.text: In that day, says the LORD, there will be the noise of a cry from the fish gate, a wailing from the second quarter, and a great crashing from the hills.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says there will be a cry from the fish gate, wailing from the second quarter, and crashing from the hills. Arminian readers see judgment reaching every part of Jerusalem, so that no district is spared.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the specific places as making the judgment vivid and real. Both traditions note that the fish gate and second quarter were areas of the city (compare Nehemiah 3:3 and 2 Kings 22:14).

verses.text: Wail, you inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the people of Canaan are undone! All those who were loaded with silver are cut off.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the inhabitants of Maktesh to wail, for the merchants are undone and those loaded with silver are cut off. Arminians see wealth gained without righteousness offering no protection in the day of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s judgment on economic injustice. Both traditions note that Maktesh may have been a market district and that the people of Canaan here likely means traders, and they hold the details loosely.

verses.text: It will happen at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are settled on their dregs, who say in their heart, “The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will search Jerusalem with lamps and punish those settled on their dregs who say he will do neither good nor evil. Arminian readers see practical unbelief, living as if God does not act, as a dangerous complacency.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the denial of God’s active rule as a serious sin. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: God sees and acts, and the image of wine left on its dregs pictures people grown thick and careless.

verses.text: Their wealth will become a plunder, and their houses a desolation. Yes, they will build houses, but won’t inhabit them. They will plant vineyards, but won’t drink their wine.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says their wealth will be plundered, their houses desolate, and they will build and plant but not enjoy the results. Arminians see the covenant curses coming true for a people who turned from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness to the warnings of the covenant (compare Deuteronomy 28:30, 39). Both traditions read the verse as showing the futility of trusting in possessions.
